title: Dynamic Belief Networks and Deep-Thinking Probes for Multi-agent Social Reasoning
summary: This paper proposes a framework combining a Dynamic Belief Network (DBN) and a Deep-Thinking Token Ratio (DTR) probe to address recursive agreement and deception detection in multi-agent LLM systems, tested in nine-player Werewolf with 3000 simulated games. DBN uses EMA smoothing to track suspicion, while DTR uses logit-lens to measure cognitive load. Results show that combining DBN with MaKTO-Proxy raises villager win rate from 44.2% to 68.8%, and adding DTR further improves vote accuracy but reduces survival, indicating a non-monotonic relationship between individual capability and collective payoff, analogous to the handicap principle.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: The paper introduces LLMs in multi-agent systems, highlighting social deduction games as testbeds for Theory of Mind. It critiques existing systems for assuming static dialogue history, leading to recursive consensus and echo chambers. It cites prior work on belief modeling and DTR, and proposes integrating probabilistic belief tracking with cross-model reasoning probes.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.content: The experimental setup uses nine-player Werewolf on AgentScope with DeepSeek-V3.2, six configurations (A-F) varying MaKTO-Proxy, DBN, and DTR modules, each playing 500 games. DBN updates suspicion via EMA with alpha=0.3, and DTR uses Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct to compute layerwise JSD as a cognitive load proxy.

sections.heading: Results and analysis
sections.content: Baseline win rate is 44.2%, rising to 68.8% with MaKTO+DBN (Group E). Vote accuracy increases monotonically from 35.5% to 66.6% (Group F). DBN improves Brier Score convergence. DTR adds vote accuracy gains but reduces survival. Alpha sensitivity shows 0.3 is optimal. DTR distributions show werewolves have higher density peaks.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.content: Group F has highest vote accuracy but lower win rate than E due to early elimination, interpreted via signaling theory and the handicap principle. MaKTO and DBN are orthogonal, with DTR providing context-dependent gains. Cross-model DTR is exploratory but shows promise.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.content: The hybrid system improves win rate and vote accuracy, with orthogonal contributions from DBN and MaKTO. The full-module configuration reveals a capability-survival conflict. Limitations include single game and homogeneous backends; future work includes Bayesian DBN, dynamic alpha, and heterogeneous agents.

method_summary: The framework uses a Dynamic Belief Network (DBN) that maintains per-player suspicion estimates via exponential moving average (EMA) smoothing with alpha=0.3, updating each round. A Deep-Thinking Token Ratio (DTR) probe computes the average Jensen-Shannon divergence between layerwise logit-lens distributions of a separate probe model (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct) to estimate cognitive load. Six configurations (A-F) combine MaKTO-Proxy (few-shot chain-of-thought), DBN, and DTR. Experiments run 500 games per configuration in nine-player Werewolf with DeepSeek-V3.2 agents.
open_questions: How does the framework generalize to other social deduction games like Avalon or Diplomacy?
Can Bayesian-based DBN with dynamic alpha scheduling improve performance further?
How does heterogeneous agent populations affect the capability-survival trade-off?
What is the optimal balance between information exposure and reasoning enhancement in multi-agent strategy design?
Can cross-model DTR be improved to reduce overlap between roles and increase discriminability?
